title: RL Transients
description: How inductor currents build up and decay with time constant L/R, and the general first-order solution.

study.title: Current build-up
study.body: The switch closes at $t = 0$, connecting a DC source through $R$ to an inductor with $i(0^-) = 0$. The inductor current cannot jump, so it starts at 0 and rises exponentially towards its DC steady-state value $V_s/R$ (inductor = short).

study.title: Inductor voltage
study.body: At $t = 0^+$ the current is still 0, so there is no drop across $R$ and the full source voltage appears across the inductor (it acts like an **open circuit**). The voltage then decays as the current builds up.

study.title: Current decay
study.body: An inductor carrying $I_0$ that is switched across a resistance $R$ keeps the current flowing in the same direction while it decays to zero. All the stored energy $\tfrac12LI_0^2$ ends up as heat in the resistance.

study.title: General first-order solution
study.body: The solution of a first-order circuit is the sum of a **particular** (forced) solution $x_p(t)$, which follows the source, and a **complementary** (natural) part $Ke^{-t/\tau}$. With DC sources $x_p$ is the constant final value, and $K$ comes from the initial condition. This works for any current or voltage in the circuit.

study.title: Initial values with switches
study.body:
- Find $i_L(0^-)$ from the DC steady state **before** switching (inductor = short).
- Continuity: $i_L(0^+) = i_L(0^-)$.
- Other quantities (resistor voltages, $v_L$) may jump. Find them at $0^+$ by replacing the inductor with a current source of value $i_L(0^+)$.
- $\tau = L/R_t$ with $R_t$ the Thévenin resistance seen by the inductor **after** switching.

study.title: Common pitfalls
study.body:
- $\tau = L/R$, **not** $LR$: a larger resistance makes an RL circuit **faster** (the opposite of RC).
- The continuous quantity is the inductor **current**, not its voltage.
- Interrupting an inductor current into a large resistance gives a large voltage spike $i_L(0^+)\cdot R$. Real circuits add a flyback diode across relay coils for this reason.

steps.title: Closing the switch
steps.body: The switch closes at $t = 0$. The inductor current starts at 0 (it cannot jump) and rises exponentially towards $V_s/R$, where the inductor finally acts as a short circuit. The time constant of an RL circuit is $\tau = L/R$.

steps.prompt: Find the time constant of an RL circuit with $L$ = {{L|H}} and $R$ = {{R|Ω}}.
The switch closes at $t = 0$. What is the inductor current a long time after the switch closes?
steps.explanation: In DC steady state the inductor is a short circuit, so only $R$ limits the current: $i(\infty) = V_s/R$.

steps.prompt: Just after the switch closes ($t = 0^+$), an inductor that carried no current behaves like an open circuit.
steps.explanation: True. Its current is still 0 at $t = 0^+$ (continuity), yet it has a voltage across it: zero current with a voltage is an open circuit. In fact $v_L(0^+) = V_s$.

steps.title: The inductor voltage decays
steps.body: Because $i$ rises along an exponential, its slope, and therefore $v_L = L\,di/dt$, decays: it starts at $V_s$ and falls to zero. KVL checks out at every instant: $Ri + v_L = V_s$.

steps.prompt: The switch closes at $t = 0$ ($i(0^-) = 0$). Find the current $i$ at $t$ = {{t|s}}.
steps.explanation: $\tau = L/R$ = {{L|H}} / {{R|Ω}} = {{tau|s}}, so $t/\tau$ = {{t/tau}}. Final current $V_s/R$ = {{Vs/R|A}}. $i = \frac{V_s}{R}(1 - e^{-t/\tau})$ = {{Vs/R|A}} × (1 − {{exp(-t/tau)}}) = {{Vs/R*(1-exp(-t/tau))|A}}.

steps.prompt: Same kind of circuit: the switch closes at $t = 0$. Find the inductor voltage $v_L$ (polarity as shown) at $t$ = {{t|s}}.
steps.explanation: $\tau = L/R$ = {{tau|s}}, $t/\tau$ = {{t/tau}}. $v_L = V_se^{-t/\tau}$ = {{Vs|V}} × {{exp(-t/tau)}} = {{Vs*exp(-t/tau)|V}}. Check with KVL: the resistor has {{Vs*(1-exp(-t/tau))|V}}, and the two add up to {{Vs|V}}.

steps.prompt: The switch closes at $t = 0$ and connects a DC source $V_s$ through $R$ to an inductor with $i(0^-) = 0$. Which graph shows the inductor voltage $v_L(t)$?
steps.explanation: The inductor current cannot jump, so at $0^+$ it is still 0 and there is no voltage across $R$: the full $V_s$ appears across $L$ (it acts like an open circuit). As the current builds up, more voltage drops across $R$, and $v_L = V_se^{-t/\tau}$ decays to 0 (in DC steady state the inductor is a short). The rising curve is the current $i(t)$.

steps.prompt: Which expression is the time constant of a series RL circuit?
steps.explanation: $\tau = L/R$ (henries/ohms = seconds). Check with intuition: a bigger $L$ resists change more and slows things down; a bigger $R$ makes the final current smaller, so it is reached sooner.

steps.prompt: An inductor $L$ = {{L|H}} carrying {{I0|A}} at $t = 0$ is switched across a resistor $R$ = {{R|Ω}}. Find the current at $t$ = {{T|s}}.
The switch closes at $t = 0$. Find the time constant of the circuit after switching.
steps.explanation: Zero the source (short it) and look from the inductor: $R_1$ and $R_2$ are in parallel, $R_t$ = {{par(R1,R2)|Ω}}. $\tau = L/R_t$ = {{L|H}} / {{par(R1,R2)|Ω}} = {{L/par(R1,R2)|s}}.

steps.prompt: The switch closes at $t = 0$ ($i_L(0^-) = 0$). Find $i_L$ at $t$ = {{t|s}}.
steps.explanation:
Final value: the inductor shorts out $R_2$, so $i_L(\infty) = V_s/R_1$ = {{Vs/R1|A}}. $R_t = R_1 \parallel R_2$ = {{par(R1,R2)|Ω}}, $\tau$ = {{tau|s}}.
$i_L = i_L(\infty)(1 - e^{-t/\tau})$ = {{Vs/R1|A}} × (1 − {{exp(-t/tau)}}) = {{Vs/R1*(1-exp(-t/tau))|A}}.

steps.prompt: In a series RL circuit ($L$ = {{L|H}}, $R$ = {{R|Ω}}) a DC source is switched on at $t = 0$ with zero initial current. How long until the current reaches {{p*100}} % of its final value?
After a switching event at $t = 0$, an inductor current has $i(0^+)$ = {{Ii|A}}, final value $i(\infty)$ = {{If|A}} and time constant $\tau$ = {{tau|s}}. Find $i$ at $t$ = {{t|s}}.
Match RC and RL facts
steps.explanation: Capacitor voltage and inductor current are the quantities tied to stored energy ($\frac12Cv^2$, $\frac12Li^2$), so they cannot jump. The time constants are $RC$ and $L/R$.

steps.prompt: An inductor $L$ = {{L|H}} carries {{I0|A}} when it is switched across a resistor. How much energy does the resistor dissipate until the current has decayed to zero?
steps.explanation: All of the inductor's stored energy ends up as heat: $w = \tfrac12LI_0^2$ = 0.5 × {{L|H}} × ({{I0|A}})² = {{0.5*L*I0^2|J}}. The resistance value only changes how quickly that happens.

steps.prompt: A {{Vs|V}} DC source is switched on at $t = 0$ across $R$ and $L$ in series ($i(0^-) = 0$). The graph shows the current. Find $L$.
steps.hint: The final current gives $R$; the time to reach 63 % of it gives $\tau$.
steps.explanation: Final value: $i(\infty) = V_s/R$ = {{If|A}}, so $R$ = {{Vs}} V / {{If|A}} = {{R|Ω}}. The current reaches 63.2 % of that, {{0.632*If|A}}, at $t = \tau$ = {{tau|s}}. Since $\tau = L/R$: $L = \tau R$ = {{tau|s}} × {{R|Ω}} = {{tau*R|H}}.

steps.prompt: The switch has been **closed** for a long time and **opens** at $t = 0$. Find the voltage $v_a(0^+)$ of node a with respect to ground just after the switch opens. Include the sign.
steps.explanation: Before opening, $L$ shorts $R_2$: $i_L(0^-) = V_s/R_1$ = {{Vs/R1|A}} (downward through $L$). After opening, this current must keep flowing; its only path is the loop $L$–$R_2$, so it flows **upward** through $R_2$. Hence $v_a(0^+) = -i_L(0^+)R_2$ = −{{Vs/R1|A}} × {{R2|Ω}} = {{-Vs*R2/R1|V}}. In magnitude that is {{R2/R1}} times $V_s$: the inductive kick.

steps.prompt: Same circuit: the switch has been closed for a long time and opens at $t = 0$. Find $i_L$ (direction shown) at $t$ = {{t|s}}.
steps.explanation: $i_L(0^+) = i_L(0^-) = V_s/R_1$ = {{Vs/R1|A}}. After opening, $L$ sees only $R_2$: $\tau = L/R_2$ = {{tau|s}}, and $i_L(\infty) = 0$. $i_L$ = {{Vs/R1|A}} × {{exp(-t/tau)}} = {{Vs/R1*exp(-t/tau)|A}}.

steps.prompt: The switch (across $R_2$) has been open for a long time and **closes** at $t = 0$. Find the current $i$ at $t$ = {{t|s}}.
steps.explanation:
Initial: $i(0^+) = i(0^-) = \frac{V_s}{R_1+R_2}$ = {{Vs/(R1+R2)|A}}. Final: $R_2$ is shorted, $i(\infty) = V_s/R_1$ = {{Vs/R1|A}}. Time constant after switching: $\tau = L/R_1$ = {{tau|s}}.
$i = i(\infty) + [i(0^+) - i(\infty)]e^{-t/\tau}$ = {{Vs/R1|A}} − {{Vs/R1 - Vs/(R1+R2)|A}} × {{exp(-t/tau)}} = {{Vs/R1 + (Vs/(R1+R2) - Vs/R1)*exp(-t/tau)|A}}.

steps.prompt: After a switch operates at $t = 0$, the inductor current follows the graph. With $L$ = {{L|H}}, find the Thévenin resistance $R_t$ the inductor sees after switching.
steps.explanation: Read $i_L(0^+)$ = {{Ii|A}} and $i_L(\infty)$ = {{If|A}}. After one time constant 63.2 % of the change is done: $i_L(\tau) = i_L(\infty) + 0.368\,[i_L(0^+) - i_L(\infty)]$ = {{If+0.368*(Ii-If)|A}}, which the curve reaches at $t$ = {{tau|s}}. Then $R_t = L/\tau$ = {{L|H}} / {{tau|s}} = {{L/tau|Ω}}.

steps.prompt: Put the steps for finding $i_L(t)$ after a switch operates in order
items: Find $i_L(0^-)$ with the inductor as a short (circuit before switching)
Find $i_L(\infty)$ in the circuit after switching
Find $R_t$ seen by the inductor and $\tau = L/R_t$
steps.explanation: Same recipe as for RC circuits, with the inductor current as the continuous quantity and $\tau = L/R_t$ instead of $R_tC$.

steps.prompt: After switching at $t = 0$, an RL circuit ($L$ = {{L|H}}, $R_t$ = {{R|Ω}}) has $i_L(0^+)$ = −{{I0|A}} and $i_L(\infty)$ = +{{If|A}}. At what time does $i_L$ pass through zero?
steps.explanation: Set $0 = I_f + (-I_0 - I_f)e^{-t/\tau}$, which gives $t = \tau\ln\frac{I_0+I_f}{I_f}$. With $\tau = L/R_t$ = {{L/R|s}}: $t$ = {{L/R|s}} × ln({{(I0+If)/If}}) = {{L/R*ln((I0+If)/If)|s}}.

steps.prompt: The voltage across an inductor can change instantaneously when a switch operates.
steps.explanation: True. Only the inductor **current** must be continuous. The voltage $L\,di/dt$ can jump, for example from 0 to $V_s$ when a source is switched on, or to a large negative value when the current is interrupted.
